items.title: A Rs 5,000 spending cap. A fleet of Defenders, Thars. Welcome to the DUSU election
items.summary: Walking out of Gate Number 4 of the Vishwavidyalaya metro station, students are met with a familiar sight during Delhi University’s election season: pamphlets and posters carrying the names and ballot numbers of ABVP, NSUI and other candidates. But DU’s election guidelines prohibit candidates from using printed campaign material. Newslaundry found that some of the posters being used for canvassing appear handwritten but are actually printed on low-quality paper. Printing shops told us that thousands of such copies can be produced for a relatively low cost. The campaign spectacle extends beyond pamphlets. Early this week, North Campus saw rows of Defenders, Scorpios and Thars being used in rallies, while students also described food, gifts, trips and other outreach activities organised by student groups. The scale of these campaigns raises questions about how the rules governing DU student elections are being followed. Under the 2005 JM Lyngdoh Committee recommendations , accepted by the Supreme Court for implementation in college and university elections, candidates may not use printed posters, pamphlets or other printed campaign material, while handmade posters are permitted only at notified campus locations. Vehicles and loudspeakers are barred from canvassing; processions and public meetings are restricted, requiring prior permission and no disruption to academic activities; and candidates are liable for defacement of campus property. The Lyngdoh committee recommendations also cap election spending at Rs 5,000 per candidate and permit funding only through voluntary contributions from the student body. Newslaundry found that these rules were flouted in the run-up to this year’s polls. On September 17, the Delhi High Court agreed to hear a plea alleging widespread violations of the Lyngdoh Committee’s recommendations and anti-defacement guidelines, among other concerns. Garbage piling up during campaign season A repeat of 2024? This is not the first time campaign material has led to questions over election rules. In September 2024, these posters became a cause to pause the election results. The court had noted prima facie violations of the Lyngdoh Committee recommendations, including allegations of excessive spending and widespread defacement during campaigning. items.title: Tryst with the Constitution: The many constitutional questions in the CJP protest order
items.summary: Earlier this month, the Supreme Court issued an order quashing all FIRs registered across India in connection with the student protest led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). It permitted the Central government and the Delhi Police to register fresh FIRs with respect to 2,873 individuals having serious criminal antecedents. While the order largely brought to a close criminal proceedings arising out of the protests, its reasoning raises several constitutional questions. Inadequate reasons for quashing the FIRs The Court’s order was passed in applications moved by the Delhi Police and other State governments, which sought the quashing of FIRs registered between July 20-25, during the student protests. Under ordinary circumstances and procedure, a party seeking the quashing of an FIR would be required to approach the respective High Court . However, in this case, the State approached the Supreme Court directly and sought invocation of its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution . The provision enables the Court to pass any order necessary “for doing complete justice” in a matter pending before it. In the past, the Court has used this extraordinary power to quash criminal proceedings, provided the principles governing the exercise of this power are complied with. These principles require that while exercising the power to quash criminal proceedings, the Court must bear in mind the nature and effect of the offence on the conscious of society, the seriousness of the injury, the voluntary nature of the compromise between the accused and the victim, and the conduct of the accused. The Court has also cautioned that the power must be exercised carefully and, in cases where High Courts have exercised similar powers mechanically and without an application of mind, it set aside their orders. A good example of its use comes from the judgment in Ramgopal and Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2021), authored by Justice Surya Kant himself. In this case, the appellants were convicted for offences under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. They sought quashing of proceedings by invoking Article 142. The Court undertook a detailed discussion of the above-mentioned principles, applied them to the proceedings and, thereafter, quashed them. The present order departs from this orderly approach. items.title: Equal pay for equal work cannot be applied mechanically; experience must be considered: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court recently held that identical job functions and duties alone do not entitle employees to claim "equal pay for equal work" under Article 14 of the Constitution [ GP Sangeetha v. State of Kerala & Ors. ]. A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu upheld a higher pay scale for teachers appointed via promotion or transfer due to their prior service experience. Legal standard for pay parity has changed over the years, the Bench remarked. "In the last century, this Court treated equal pay for equal work as an expansive anti-exploitation principle under Articles 14 and 39(d), where the mere sameness of designation was sufficient to claim parity. In this century, however, the doctrine has been recast as a strict test based on service rules. Decisions are legion that equal pay cannot be claimed by merely showing identical work; the claimant-employee must establish complete parity in the source of recruitment, educational qualifications and experience," the Court said. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu The Court was hearing appeals filed by directly recruited junior higher secondary school teachers challenging a March 2011 judgment of the Kerala High Court. The High Court's Division Bench had reversed a single-judge order, and held that promotee teachers formed a distinct class as they were previously full-time permanent lower school teachers with long service. Granting them full-time pay scales was a valid recognition of their past service and status protection unlike direct recruits who entered as freshers, the High Court said. Aggrieved by the decision, the directly recruited teachers approached the Supreme Court. Before the apex court, the teachers argued that direct recruits and promotees perform identical duties with equal workloads, and maintaining disparity in pay scales within the same cadre amounted to grave discrimination. However, the Supreme Court rejected the contention and noted that mechanical application of the equal pay doctrine must be eschewed. "Article 14 permits reasonable classification based on qualities or characteristics of persons recruited and grouped together. In service matters, merit or experience can be a proper basis for classification for the purposes of pay in order to promote efficiency in administration," the Court stated, quoting settled precedents. items.title: Fear of court intervention must not stop arbitrators from taking a firm stand: Ciccu Mukhopadhaya
items.summary: Arbitrators should not become hesitant in controlling proceedings merely because they fear that a court may later set aside their award, Senior Advocate Ciccu Mukhopadhaya said on Thursday. Mukhopadhaya said arbitral institutions can help curb delay tactics, but the ultimate responsibility rests with the tribunal. “ It is entirely the job of the Tribunal to control. The Tribunal must have the confidence in itself and not really bother that if the court tomorrow is going to set it aside, so be it. But if you give a well-reasoned order as to why you think the Party should be denied that opportunity again and again, then the court is unlikely that the court will ultimately interfere with it .” The panel was moderated by Shantanu Agarwal, Managing Partner, Lexster Law . It also included Senior Advocate Mahesh Jethmalani , Mahmood Hussain, Founding Partner, M&Co Legal, Dubai , and Olga Tsvetkova, Managing Partner, Brevia Legal, Abu Dhabi, UAE . Mukhopadhyay said parties could delay arbitration at virtually every stage, from appointment of arbitrators and filing of pleadings to document production and adjournment requests. Mukhopadhaya pointed to instances where parties withheld key documents during pleadings and later filed thousands of pages shortly before witness examination. He said he had seen parties suddenly file 10,000 pages at the evidence stage, leaving the other side little time to prepare for rebuttal statements or cross-examination. He said, “ A Tribunal that enforces the timetable from the very first filing sets the tone for the entire proceeding. One that indulges the first extension has already lost control of the last. ” He suggested that costs be imposed at procedural milestones rather than being deferred until the final award. The organisation said three of its members were injured, two with head wounds and one with a fractured hand. items.summary: The Supreme Court recently held that a litigant cannot be denied relief merely on account of a delay in filing an appeal when the delay is caused entirely by a fault on a tribunal or court's e-filing portal [ Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms Mamta Binani and Others ]. A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu made the observation in a case where an appeal in an insolvency resolution case was filed with a delay of one day because earlier attempts to e-file the appeal failed due to glitches on the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal's (NCLAT) online portal. “ Should a litigant be shown the door at the very first instance due to e-filing of an appeal beyond the statutorily condonable period, particularly when such a filing has been delayed for bona fide reasons beyond the litigant’s control and when the fault was entirely at the end of the Registry of the NCLAT? We think not! ” the Supreme Court said in its September 10 ruling. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu Supreme Court Should a litigant be shown the door when a filing has been delayed for bona fide reasons beyond the litigant’s control, when the fault was entirely at the end of the Registry of the NCLAT? We think not! The Bench also invoked the principle of actus curiae neminem gravabit , which means that an act of the court should prejudice no one. “ When the system of the court/tribunal fails to receive the papers, which are sought to be presented bona fide and within the prescribed time, the litigant cannot be rendered remediless on the specious ground that the court/tribunal has no power to condone the delay, ” the judgment stated. The matter before the Court was tied to insolvency proceedings concerning Rolta India Limited. " The convict was a senior officer of the Indian Police Service and had held several responsible positions during his service career, including 145 the rank of Director General of Police, Kerala. The higher the public office held, greater is the obligation to maintain the highest standards of integrity and probity. The disproportion of ₹30,84,892.39, constituting 52.33% of the known income, is neither marginal nor insignificant. While Thachankary requested for a lighter sentence citing medical ailments, the Court opined that his position did not warrant leniency especially considering the magnitude of his abuse of power. items.title: Bengaluru man throws acid on wife, brutally attacks her with knife in full public view
items.summary: Madhumitha, a 26-year-old nurse, had stepped out of the clinic for breakfast on Thursday, September 17, when her husband chased her down, attacked her with a butcher knife and poured acid on her. The attack took place in full public view around 9.15 am near Narayana Clinic in Bengaluru’s JP Nagar. Madhumitha is currently undergoing treatment at a private hospital. She is in a critical condition, according to the police. Madhumitha, who hails from Kolkata, has been working at the clinic for around one-and-a-half years. According to sources, Madhumitha and Venkatesh were married in 2023 and had been living separately for the past year due to family disputes. The alleged attack is suspected to have followed marital differences between the couple. Venkatesh had arrived at the clinic on a motorcycle carrying a knife, a machete and acid. Madhumitha had reportedly stepped out of the clinic to have breakfast at around 9.15 am when he followed her. She reached the hospital parking area while shouting for help, where the accused repeatedly attacked her with a machete and another sharp weapon before pouring floor-cleaning acid on her. A video from the spot shows Madhumitha, wearing a purple scrub, lying on the sloped entrance of a parking area, with blood pouring from her head and neck. Another video shows a man identified as Venkatesh, wearing a dark grey T-shirt, dark trousers and a blue cap, standing over her and repeatedly attacking her with a knife. The video appears to show him stabbing her around the head and neck. People around reportedly attempted to intervene and rescue Madhumitha. They threw stones at Venkatesh when he continued attacking her. The accused also allegedly attempted to attack those who came to her rescue. Traffic police personnel stationed at a nearby signal subsequently took Venkatesh into custody and handed him over to the JP Nagar police.

items.summary: On September 13 2026, Umar Khalid’s still images filled many of our timelines. It was this day, six years ago, that Dr Umar Khalid was jailed and put in the Tihar prison. Prisoner number 626710 is Present , Lalit Vachani’s film, narrates and narrativises the wrongful and unjust journey in which the bright scholar, also a passionate activist, and a playful, humorous friend to many, was easily deemed an ‘anti-national’. The film chronicles how, through mainstream media and organised cyber cell-constructed narratives, the struggles of resistance led by students and citizens of this country were vilified. It cautions against the robbing of a dream– a dream of an independent country, built on the principles of equality, liberty and fraternity, enshrined in the Constitution. The most alive parts of the film are undoubtedly Umar Khalid addressing various crowds across the country, holding onto every opportunity in the making of a public that is aware, or fundamentally, even in the making of a discerning public as against a mob. In all of these speeches, not strategically, but passionately, he professes his love for this country and its democratic traditions that stand on the Constitution’s ideals. In fact, Shuddhabrata Sengupta, an artist part of the RAQS Media Collective, writer, the “messy older brother” friend of Umar Khalid (as he describes himself in the film later), points this out: “Umar, when he says, 'If they spread hatred, we will respond with love’, really means it in an empirical sense and not rhetorically.” Yet, even a screening of the film is banned from public universities and campuses; screenings get cancelled at the very last minute, in the name of strategy, anonymous and informal pressure from the top, and the measured limits of dialogue. The fear is real, and it looms above and around us. items.title: Former Kerala DGP Tomin Thachankary sentenced to 4 years in disproportionate assets case
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A Kerala Vigilance Court on Thursday, September 17, sentenced former Kerala Director General of Police (DGP) Tomin J Thachankary to four years of rigorous imprisonment in a long-running disproportionate assets case. The Special Court in Kottayam also imposed a fine of Rs 30.84 lakh on him. The case was registered in 2007, after Thachankary was promoted as a Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of Police. The VACB filed the chargesheet in 2013, by which time he had been promoted to Additional Director General of Police (ADGP). The allegations are that Thachankary accumulated assets worth Rs 64.7 lakh between January 2003 and July 2007. According to a LiveLaw report , the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) found that the assets he acquired during this period were between 135% and 138% disproportionate to his known sources of official income. Thachankary had maintained that the assets under scrutiny were acquired through family partition, inheritance and gifts. He sought discharge from the case on those grounds, but the Vigilance Court rejected his plea in May 2020, holding that there was prima facie material to proceed with the trial. In January 2021, the Kerala government sanctioned a further investigation by a separate special unit of the VACB following a representation from Thachankary. Anti-corruption activist Bobby Kuruvila subsequently approached the Kerala High Court, alleging that the government's decision was intended to delay the trial. In August 2025, a Division Bench of the Kerala High Court set aside the government's order and directed that the trial be completed within a time-bound period. Thachankary, a 1987-batch IPS officer of the Kerala cadre, retired in 2023 as DGP (Investigation) of the Kerala State Human Rights Commission. During his career, he served in several prominent positions, including Managing Director of Kerala Marketfed and Consumerfed, Chairman and Managing Director of the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC), CMD of the Kerala Books and Publications Society, and Chief of the Kerala Fire and Rescue Services.

items.summary: Karnataka authorities relieved Dr Ankita R Yaragal, niece of Bagalkot Congress MLA Umesh Meti, from her post as a medical officer at a Namma Clinic, on Thursday, September 17, after allegations that she was drawing a monthly salary of Rs 75,000 while pursuing an MD course at a private medical college. Dr Ankita was appointed as a contractual medical officer at the Namma Clinic in Wambe Colony in Bagalkot town in April 2025. She is the daughter of Bagalkot District Health Officer (DHO) Dr Rajkumar Yaragal. The matter came to light after Bagalkot Taluk Health Officer (THO) Dr Saraswati Magi visited the clinic a few days ago and found Dr Ankita absent. When contacted over the phone, she reportedly said that she was out of station. Patients allegedly told the THO that the doctor had not been attending the clinic for around three months, although her attendance was intact. Residents had reportedly complained that doctors were not regularly attending the Namma Clinic and that nurses were managing patients and dispensing medicines. Dr Ankita had joined an MD programme in Pathology at a private medical college in March 2026 while continuing to serve as a medical officer at the Namma Clinic. Reports said she was drawing a monthly salary of Rs 75,000. Bagalkot Zilla Panchayat CEO Gajanan Bale directed that Dr Ankita be relieved from service after the allegations came to light. Bale said, “I have sought a report from the DHO, and action will be initiated.” Dr Ankita was also summoned for an inquiry by Bale but did not appear. She has been directed to attend another hearing on September 18 at 10 am at the Zilla Panchayat office. The inquiry is examining allegations that she was simultaneously pursuing the postgraduate course and working as a medical officer, as well as allegations regarding her absence from the clinic. The notice issued by the Bagalkot Zilla Panchayat CEO states that the principal of SN Medical College had granted Dr Ankita permission to pursue the course. However, it alleges that she continued to remain absent from her duties at the Namma Clinic. The notice also stated that disciplinary action could be initiated if the allegations are established. The matter could also be referred to the Karnataka Medical Council and the National Medical Commission. items.summary: Outdoor birthday parties come with a problem indoor ones don't have to deal with, heat, wind, and the very real risk of a beautifully frosted cake turning into a puddle before anyone's had a slice. Picking the right cake format matters just as much as picking the flavour when the celebration is happening in a garden, a park, or under a tent rather than a climate-controlled living room. The good news is that being outdoors-friendly doesn't have to mean boring. A few smart format choices can hold up in warmer weather while still looking festive enough for photos. If you're browsing options and want something specifically built for a child's celebration, a solid birthday cake for kids range usually includes a few formats that travel and hold up well outdoors, which is worth checking before settling on a design purely based on looks. Here are seven ideas worth considering, starting with the simplest options and moving toward ones that need a bit more planning. 7 Cake Ideas That Hold Up Outdoors 1. Sheet Cakes Another good option for an outside party is a simple sheet cake. The reason for this is the fact that this type of cake does not have several layers, which may bend in the heat. Another reason why this cake is a good choice is that it can serve many people without slicing it into pieces. 2. Cupcakes Instead of a Single Cake Cupcakes solve two outdoor problems at once, portion control and heat exposure. Since each one is individually wrapped in its own liner, they hold their shape better than a large frosted cake left out in the sun, and serving them doesn't require a knife, a table, or careful cutting in front of a crowd of restless kids. This is one of the simplest formats to find within a birthday cake for kids selection, since cupcakes are almost always available in playful, kid-friendly designs. 3. Naked or Semi-Naked Cakes Without much outer frosting or only a thin layer of frosting between the sponge and a small amount of frosting on top, the cake becomes much more stable in warmer conditions because there is less buttercream that will melt, and at the same time, the layers appear on purpose. 4.
